turns.question: How can I appeal an account suspension?

facts: Direct users to the Appeal and Reinstatement form; do not promise success.

response.answer:
To contest an account suspension, submit the Appeal and Reinstatement form — GitHub's internal complaint-handling process for reinstatement requests and appeals of moderation decisions [1][2][3].

Two paths exist, depending on your situation [4]:
- **Reinstatement** — you want access back, are willing to make any necessary changes to address the violation, and agree not to violate the terms going forward [4].
- **Appeal** — you dispute that a violation occurred and can provide additional information showing a different decision should have been reached [4].

Timing: you may appeal a moderation decision for up to six months after the decision; GitHub may, in its discretion, refuse to consider appeals submitted later than that [5].

Review process: GitHub staff review the information in the form to determine whether it is sufficient to warrant reinstatement or granting the appeal [5]. All legitimate reinstatement requests are reviewed initially by GitHub staff and answered with a decision [6], though reinstatement depends on the circumstances and severity of the initial violation [6].

turns.question: What does reinstatement mean under GitHub policy?

facts: Regain access while agreeing to necessary changes and future compliance.

Under GitHub's Appeal and Reinstatement policy, a "Reinstatement" is where a user wishes to regain access to their account or content and is willing to make any necessary changes to address the violation and agrees not to violate GitHub's terms going forward [1]. Both arise from decisions to disable or limit access to content or an account — such as removing or restricting content, suspending or terminating account access, suspending or terminating service access, or restricting the ability to monetize content [1]. - All legitimate Reinstatement requests are reviewed initially by GitHub staff and answered with a decision [3].
- Note that the six-month limit described in the policy applies specifically to Appeals, not to Reinstatements [4].

Requests are tracked publicly in GitHub's Transparency Center [5].

turns.question: Is all malware research code banned on GitHub?

facts: Dual-use research content can be allowed; do not assert a blanket ban.

response.answer:
No. GitHub explicitly allows dual-use content and supports posting content used for research into vulnerabilities, malware, or exploits, because publishing and distributing such content has educational value and provides a net benefit to the security community; GitHub says it assumes positive intention behind such projects [1].

What is prohibited is using the platform in direct support of unlawful attacks that cause technical harms — for example, delivering malicious executables or acting as attack infrastructure (DDoS organization, command-and-control servers) — where there is no implicit or explicit dual-use purpose prior to the abuse occurring [1]. The Acceptable Use Policies restate this: no content or activity that directly supports unlawful active attack or malware campaigns causing technical harms, and no using GitHub servers to disrupt or gain unauthorized access to services, devices, data, accounts or networks (bug bounty activity under a program like GitHub's Bug Bounty is not treated as unauthorized) [2].

In rare cases of very widespread abuse of dual-use content, GitHub may restrict access to that specific instance — usually by putting it behind authentication, and only as a last resort disabling access or removing it (e.g., gists) — to disrupt an ongoing unlawful attack or malware campaign; these restrictions are temporary where feasible and can be appealed [1].

For potentially harmful security research, GitHub recommends (but does not require) that repository owners add a disclaimer in the README.md or source comments identifying any potentially harmful content, and provide a contact method via a SECURITY.md file for third-party abuse inquiries [1].

One caveat: for the npm registry, GitHub considers it a platform used primarily for installation and run-time use of code, not for research [3].

We assume positive intention and use of these projects to promote and drive improvements across the ecosystem.

  In rare cases of very widespread abuse of dual-use content, we may restrict access to that specific instance of the content to disrupt an ongoing unlawful attack or malware campaign that is leveraging the GitHub platform as an exploit or malware CDN. In most of these instances, restriction takes the form of putting the content behind authentication, but may, as an option of last resort, involve disabling access or full removal where this is not possible (e.g. when posted as a gist). We will also contact the project owners about restrictions put in place where possible.

  Restrictions are temporary where feasible, and do not serve the purpose of purging or restricting any specific dual-use content, or copies of that content, from the platform in perpetuity. While we aim to make these rare cases of restriction a collaborative process with project owners, if you do feel your content was unduly restricted, we have an [appeals process](/site-policy/acceptable-use-policies/github-appeal-and-reinstatement) in place.

* Clearly identify and describe any potentially harmful content in a disclaimer in the project’s README.md file or source code comments.
* Provide a preferred contact method for any 3rd party abuse inquiries through a SECURITY.md file in the repository (e.g. "Please create an issue on this repository for any questions or concerns"). Such a contact method allows 3rd parties to reach out to project maintainers directly and potentially resolve concerns without the need to file abuse reports.

Per GitHub's Deceased User Policy, when a GitHub user passes away, GitHub can work with an authorized individual to determine what happens to the account's content [1].

turns.question: Is matching a registered trademark as a username necessarily a violation?

facts: A matching username alone is not necessarily a trademark violation.

response.answer:
No — not by itself. GitHub's Trademark Policy states explicitly that an account with a username that happens to be the same as a registered trademark is not, by itself, necessarily a violation of the trademark policy; usernames are first come, first served and may not be reserved [1]. Using another's trademark in a way unrelated to the product or service for which the mark was granted is not a trademark policy violation either [1].

What can make it a violation is misleading or confusing use: using a company/business name, logo, or other trademark-protected material in a manner that may mislead or confuse others about brand or business affiliation [2]. Separately, under the Impersonation policy you may not misrepresent your identity or association with another person or organization, including using a deceptively similar username — but a username similar to another is not necessarily impersonation, and GitHub takes context (e.g., parody and satire) into account [3].

When a validated complaint arrives, GitHub reviews the account: clear intent to mislead through unauthorized trademark use can lead to suspension and notice to the account holder, while an account that appears confusing but is not purposefully passing itself off gets an opportunity to clear up the confusion, and GitHub may release the username for the trademark holder's active use [4]. Valid trademark-related complaints are the only requests GitHub reviews for possible release of an already-claimed username [5].

turns.question: Does a DMCA takedown of the parent automatically remove all forks?

facts: Not automatically; forks should be investigated and identified; note documented exceptions if discussed.

response.answer:
No — not automatically. GitHub **will not** automatically disable forks when it disables a parent repository. The stated reasons are that forks belong to different users, may have been altered in significant ways, and may be licensed or used in a way protected by fair use; GitHub does not conduct any independent investigation into forks, and expects copyright owners to do that investigation and to expressly include forks in their takedown notice [1]. The how-to guide repeats this and asks claimants who believe forks are also infringing to explicitly identify each allegedly infringing fork and confirm that their sworn statements apply to each identified fork [2].

There are two situations where a network of forks may be processed together:

1. **All existing forks identified.** If, at the time the notice was submitted, the claimant identified all existing forks of that repository as allegedly infringing, GitHub would process a valid claim against all forks in that network at the time it processes the notice, given the likelihood that all newly created forks would contain the same content [1] [2].
2. **Networks over 100 repositories.** If the reported network is larger than one hundred (100) repositories and thus difficult to review in its entirety, GitHub may consider disabling the entire network if the notice states: "Based on the representative number of forks I have reviewed, I believe that all or most of the forks are infringing to the same extent as the parent repository" — and the claimant's sworn statement applies to that statement [1] [2].

Note that these outcomes are discretionary ("may consider"), and the parallel rule in the Private Information Removal Policy has the same structure for non-copyright reports [3].

citations.heading: B. What About Forks? (or What's a Fork?)
citations.content:
## B. What About Forks? (or What's a Fork?)

One of the best features of GitHub is the ability for users to "fork" one another's repositories. What does that mean? In essence, it means that users can make a copy of a project on GitHub into their own repositories. As the license or the law allows, users can then make changes to that fork to either push back to the main project or just keep as their own variation of a project. Each of these copies is a [AUTOTITLE](/get-started/learning-about-github/github-glossary#fork) of the original repository, which in turn may also be called the "parent" of the fork.

GitHub _will not_ automatically disable forks when disabling a parent repository. This is because forks belong to different users, may have been altered in significant ways, and may be licensed or used in a different way that is protected by the fair-use doctrine. GitHub does not conduct any independent investigation into forks. We expect copyright owners to conduct that investigation and, if they believe that the forks are also infringing, expressly include forks in their takedown notice.

In rare cases, you may be alleging copyright infringement in a full repository that is actively being forked. If at the time that you submitted your notice, you identified all existing forks of that repository as allegedly infringing, we would process a valid claim against all forks in that network at the time we process the notice. We would do this given the likelihood that all newly created forks would contain the same content. In addition, if the reported network that contains the allegedly infringing content is larger than one hundred (100) repositories and thus would be difficult to review in its entirety, we may consider disabling the entire network if you state in your notice that, "Based on the representative number of forks I have reviewed, I believe that all or most of the forks are infringing to the same extent as the parent repository." Your sworn statement would apply to this statement.

facts: Explain the appeal form.

response.answer:
To appeal a moderation decision, submit the **Appeal and Reinstatement form** (support.github.com/contact/reinstatement) [1]. GitHub runs an internal complaint-handling process for this [2].

**Timing:** You may appeal a moderation decision for up to six months after the decision; GitHub may, at its discretion, decline to consider appeals submitted later than that [1].

**Appeal vs. Reinstatement:**
- An **Appeal** disputes that a violation occurred and provides additional information showing a different decision should have been reached [3].
- A **Reinstatement** is for when you want to regain access to your account or content and are willing to make the necessary changes and agree not to violate the terms going forward [3].

These apply to decisions to remove/restrict content, suspend or terminate an account or service access, or restrict monetization [3].

**How it's reviewed:** Staff review the form to see whether there's sufficient information to warrant reinstatement or granting the appeal [1]. GitHub will reverse or modify a decision when the appeal shows (i) the decision to act or not act was mistaken, (ii) the content/conduct was not illegal and not incompatible with the Terms, or (iii) a lesser severity of action was warranted [4]. All appeal decisions are made by humans, not automated means; if the reviewer was the person who made the initial determination and is inclined to deny, a different staff member independently reviews it [4]. All legitimate appeals receive a final decision [4].

**If still unsatisfied:** In certain circumstances (e.g., in the EU under the Digital Services Act) you may have rights to seek review under local law [5].

While the majority of interactions between individuals in GitHub’s community fall within our Acceptable Use Policies and Community Guidelines, violations of those policies do occur at times. ## What are Appeals and Reinstatements?

Both Appeals and Reinstatements may arise in relation to decisions to disable or limit access to content or an account, including decisions whether or not to:

* Remove, disable access to, or restrict visibility of content
* Suspend or terminate access to an account
* Suspend or terminate access to the service, in whole or in part
* Suspend, terminate or otherwise restrict the ability to monetize content

A “Reinstatement” is where a user wishes to regain access to their account or content and is willing to make any necessary changes to address the violation and agrees not to violate our terms going forward.

An “Appeal” is where a user disputes that a violation has occurred and can provide additional information to show that a different decision should have been reached.

GitHub will reverse or modify its decision when the Appeal contains sufficient grounds for us to determine that (i) our decision to act or not to act was mistaken; (ii) that the content or conduct was not illegal and not incompatible with our Terms; or (iii) that the content or conduct warrants a lesser severity of action than the measure taken.

All decisions on Appeal are made by humans and not by any automated means. If the GitHub Staff reviewer on the Appeal is the same person who made the initial determination and that staff member believes their initial conclusion was correct (and thus would be inclined to deny the Appeal), a different member of GitHub’s staff will independently review the Appeal.

All legitimate Appeals will be answered with a final decision.

facts: Support will not restore access.

response.answer:
No — for security reasons, GitHub Support will not restore access to accounts with two-factor authentication enabled if you have lost your 2FA credentials or lost access to your account recovery methods. What you can still do:

- Unlink email addresses from the locked account so you can create a new account or use that email on another existing account [2].
- Clone or fork any public content from the lost account (and, for an organization, ask remaining members to clone/fork private content); Support will not recover the contents of a locked account [3].
- Contact Support to request removal of a payment method from a locked-out account — though this does not restore the account itself [4].

Note that you remain responsible for maintaining the security of your account, and GitHub is not liable for loss resulting from a failure to meet that security obligation [5].

turns.question: Compare posting personal information with requesting removal of leaked access credentials.

facts: Distinguish the personal-information prohibition from the specific-risk removal process.

response.answer:
They are two sides of the same policy area, but they sit in different documents and have different requirements.

**1. Posting personal information (the prohibition)**
- Posting another person's personal information without consent violates GitHub's privacy rules: content that "violates the privacy of any third party, such as by posting another person's personal information without consent" is not allowed [1].
- The Doxxing and Invasion of Privacy policy says: "Don't post other people's personal information," including private email addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses/private location info, bank account or credit card numbers, Social Security/National Identity numbers, **passwords**, voter information, medical information and biometric data, and other private information that may pose a safety or security risk [2].
- GitHub takes context into account, including whether the reported content is publicly available elsewhere; sharing publicly available content may not itself violate the policy, but sharing it with intent to harass or incite abuse may violate the bullying and harassment prohibition [2].
- Separately, misuse of personal information is prohibited, and anyone collecting personal information from the Service must only use it for the purpose the user authorized, secure it, and respond promptly to complaints, removal requests and "do not contact" requests [3].

**2. Requesting removal of leaked access credentials (the remediation path)**
- The Private Information Removal process is offered as an "exceptional service only for high-risk content," such as when your security is at risk from exposed access credentials [4].
- "Private information" for this purpose means content that (i) should have been kept confidential *and* (ii) whose public availability poses a specific or targeted security risk to you or your organization; "security risk" means exposure to physical danger, identity theft, or increased likelihood of unauthorized access to physical or network facilities [5].
- Requests are appropriate for access credentials such as usernames combined with passwords, access tokens or other sensitive secrets that grant access to your organization's server, network or domain; AWS tokens and similar credentials granting access to a third party on your behalf (you must be able to show the token belongs to you); documentation such as network diagrams posing a specific security risk; and information related to and posing a security risk to you as an individual, such as government ID numbers [6].
- Requests are *not* appropriate for internal server names, IP addresses and URLs on their own; mere mentions of your company name/brand/domain; entire files or repositories without a specific security risk; copyright or trademark matters; privacy complaints (use the privacy contact form instead); or general Community Guidelines issues [7].
- A request must include a working, clickable link to each file containing the private information (not search results, examples or screenshots), specific line numbers, and a brief description of how each item poses a security risk to you or your organization — explaining the risk beyond merely asserting it; agents acting for an organization must state their legal right to do so, and urgency (e.g., a very recent credential exposure) can optionally be flagged with a reason [8].

**Key contrast:** the first is a substantive prohibition on publishing someone else's personal data (including passwords) [2][1]; the second is a narrow removal mechanism aimed at confidential content whose exposure creates a concrete security risk, requiring you to demonstrate ownership/link, line numbers, and a specific risk explanation [6][8]. Note the overlap: passwords appear in the doxxing list [2], while credential exposure is the flagship use case for removal requests [4] — but privacy complaints generally are routed away from the removal process [7].

turns.question: Can I use a DMCA notice for a trademark dispute, or is there another route?

facts: DMCA handles copyright; trademark reports use a separate process.

response.answer:
No — the DMCA process is not the right channel for a trademark dispute. GitHub's DMCA notice-and-takedown process "should be used only for complaints about copyright infringement," and notices must identify copyrighted works that are allegedly being infringed; it cannot be used for other complaints such as alleged trademark infringement or sensitive data, for which GitHub offers separate processes [1]. The DMCA guide repeats this: GitHub can only accept DMCA takedown notices for works protected by copyright, and trademark complaints should go through the trademark policy [2].

The alternative route is GitHub's Trademark Policy. Holders of registered trademarks can report possible trademark policy violations via GitHub's Trademark Policy Violation Report form, using a company email address and clearly describing why the account may cause confusion with, or dilute/tarnish, the mark [3].

What to include in the report [4]:
- Username of the reported account
- Your company name, company GitHub account (if any), and company website
- The trademarked word/symbol, registration number, and registration office (e.g., USPTO)
- Description of the confusion (e.g., passing off as your company, with specifics)
- Requested action (e.g., removal of the violating account or transfer of a trademarked username)
- Statement: "I have a good faith belief that use of the trademark described above is not authorized by the trademark owner, or its agent, or the law. I have taken nominative and other fair uses into consideration."
- Statement: "I swear, under penalty of perjury, that the information in this notification is accurate and that I am the trademark owner, or am authorized to act on behalf of the owner, of an exclusive right that is allegedly infringed."
- Your physical or electronic signature

Note that a federal or international registration number is normally required; if the name is not a registered mark (e.g., a government agency or non-profit), the policy lists alternative contact details to provide [4].

On outcomes: for reports from holders of federal or international registrations, GitHub reviews the account and may suspend it where there is clear intent to mislead, or, where an account is confusing but not purposefully passing itself off, give the account holder a chance to clear up the confusion and possibly release the username for the trademark holder's use [5]. Valid trademark complaints are also the only requests GitHub reviews for possible release of an already-claimed username [6].

Also note the private-information removal process explicitly does not handle trademark disputes either [7]. As always, this is policy information, not legal advice.

citations.heading: DMCA Notices In a Nutshell
citations.content:
## DMCA Notices In a Nutshell

The DMCA provides two simple, straightforward procedures that all GitHub users should know about: (i) a [takedown-notice](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/guide-to-submitting-a-dmca-takedown-notice) procedure for copyright holders to request that content be removed; and (ii) a [counter-notice](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/guide-to-submitting-a-dmca-counter-notice) procedure for users to get content re-enabled when content is taken down by mistake or misidentification.

DMCA [takedown notices](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/guide-to-submitting-a-dmca-takedown-notice) are used by copyright owners to ask GitHub to take down content they believe to be infringing. If you are a software designer or developer, you create copyrighted content every day. If someone else is using your copyrighted content in an unauthorized manner on GitHub, you can send us a DMCA takedown notice to request that the infringing content be changed or removed.

On the other hand, [counter notices](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/guide-to-submitting-a-dmca-counter-notice) can be used to correct mistakes. Maybe the person sending the takedown notice does not hold the copyright or did not realize that you have a license or made some other mistake in their takedown notice. Since GitHub usually cannot know if there has been a mistake, the DMCA counter notice allows you to let us know and ask that we put the content back up.

The DMCA notice and takedown process should be used only for complaints about copyright infringement. Notices sent through our DMCA process must identify copyrighted work or works that are allegedly being infringed. The process cannot be used for other complaints, such as complaints about alleged [trademark infringement](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/github-trademark-policy) or [sensitive data](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/github-private-information-removal-policy); we offer separate processes for those situations.

citations.heading: Before You Start

## Before You Start

***Tell the Truth.*** The DMCA requires that you swear to the facts in your copyright complaint _under penalty of perjury_. It is a federal crime to intentionally lie in a sworn declaration. (_See_ [U.S. Code, Title 18, Section 1621](https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/USCODE-2011-title18/html/USCODE-2011-title18-partI-chap79-sec1621.htm).) Submitting false information could also result in civil liability — that is, you could get sued for money damages. The DMCA itself [provides for damages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_Copyright_Infringement_Liability_Limitation_Act#%C2%A7_512(f)_Misrepresentations) against any person who knowingly materially misrepresents that material or activity is infringing. <!-- markdownlint-disable-line emphasis-style -->

***Investigate.*** Millions of users and organizations pour their hearts and souls into the projects they create and contribute to on GitHub. Filing a DMCA complaint against such a project is a serious legal allegation that carries real consequences for real people. Because of that, we ask that you conduct a thorough investigation and consult with an attorney before submitting a takedown to make sure that the use isn't actually permissible. <!-- markdownlint-disable-line emphasis-style -->

***Ask Nicely First.*** A great first step before sending us a takedown notice is to try contacting the user directly. They may have listed contact information on their public profile page or in the repository's README, or you could get in touch by opening an issue or pull request on the repository. This is not strictly required, but it is classy. <!-- markdownlint-disable-line emphasis-style -->

***Send In The Correct Request.*** We can only accept DMCA takedown notices for works that are protected by copyright, and that identify a specific copyrightable work. If you have a complaint about trademark abuse, please see our [trademark policy](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/github-trademark-policy). If you wish to remove sensitive data such as passwords, please see our [policy on sensitive data](/site-policy/content-removal-policies/github-private-information-removal-policy). If you are dealing with defamation or other abusive behavior, please see our [Community Guidelines](/site-policy/github-terms/github-community-guidelines). <!-- markdownlint-disable-line emphasis-style -->

***Code Is Different From Other Creative Content.*** GitHub is built for collaboration on software code. This makes identifying a valid copyright infringement more complicated than it might otherwise be for, say, photos, music, or videos. <!-- markdownlint-disable-line emphasis-style -->

turns.question: My dual-use malware research was restricted. Is research allowed, and can I appeal?

facts: Research may be allowed; restrictions can occur; explain the appeal route without promising success.

response.answer:
**Yes — dual-use research is allowed in principle, and yes, you can appeal.**

**Research is allowed**
GitHub explicitly allows dual-use content and supports posting content used for research into vulnerabilities, malware, or exploits, because publishing and distributing such content has educational value and a net benefit to the security community; GitHub assumes positive intention for these projects [1]. What's prohibited is using GitHub in direct support of unlawful attacks causing technical harms (e.g., delivering malicious executables, denial of service, command-and-control infrastructure) with no implicit or explicit dual-use purpose prior to the abuse occurring [1] [2].

**Why a restriction can still happen**
In rare cases of very widespread abuse of dual-use content, GitHub may restrict access to that specific instance of the content to disrupt an ongoing unlawful attack or malware campaign, typically by putting the content behind authentication, and only as a last resort by disabling access or removing it (e.g., gists). Restrictions are meant to be temporary where feasible, and GitHub will contact project owners where possible [1].

**Appealing**
If you feel your content was unduly restricted, there is an appeals process [1]. turns.question: Are forks automatically removed for either copyright or private-information takedowns?

facts: Neither process automatically removes every fork; acknowledge investigation and specified exceptions.

response.answer:
No — in both processes, forks are not automatically disabled/removed when a parent repository is disabled.

**Copyright (DMCA):** GitHub will not automatically disable forks when disabling a parent repository, because forks belong to different users, may have been altered significantly, and may be licensed or used in ways protected by fair use; GitHub does not independently investigate forks and expects the copyright owner to do so and to expressly include forks in the notice [1]. The notice guide repeats this: if you believe forks are also infringing, you must explicitly identify each allegedly infringing fork and confirm you investigated each case [2]. Two exceptions where forks can be covered: if at the time of submission you identified all existing forks as allegedly infringing, GitHub would process a valid claim against all forks in that network when processing the notice; and for networks larger than 100 repositories that would be difficult to review in their entirety, GitHub may consider disabling the entire network if the notice states, "Based on the representative number of forks you have reviewed, I believe that all or most of the forks are infringing to the same extent as the parent repository" [1].

**Private information:** GitHub likewise will not automatically disable forks when disabling a parent repository, since forks belong to different users and may have been altered [3]. Senders of private-information removal requests are expected to investigate and expressly include forks in their request [3]. If all existing forks were identified at submission time, GitHub would process a valid claim against all forks in the network at the time it processes the notice; and for networks over 100 repositories that would be hard to review fully, GitHub may consider disabling the entire network if the notice states that, based on the representative number of forks reviewed, all or most forks contain the content reported in the parent repository [3].

## B. What About Forks? (or What's a Fork?)

One of the best features of GitHub is the ability for users to "fork" one another's repositories. What does that mean? In essence, it means that users can make a copy of a project on GitHub into their own repositories. As the license or the law allows, users can then make changes to that fork to either push back to the main project or just keep as their own variation of a project. Each of these copies is a [AUTOTITLE](/get-started/learning-about-github/github-glossary#fork) of the original repository, which in turn may also be called the "parent" of the fork.

GitHub _will not_ automatically disable forks when disabling a parent repository. This is because forks belong to different users, may have been altered in significant ways, and may be licensed or used in a different way that is protected by the fair-use doctrine. GitHub does not conduct any independent investigation into forks. We expect copyright owners to conduct that investigation and, if they believe that the forks are also infringing, expressly include forks in their takedown notice.

In rare cases, you may be alleging copyright infringement in a full repository that is actively being forked. If at the time that you submitted your notice, you identified all existing forks of that repository as allegedly infringing, we would process a valid claim against all forks in that network at the time we process the notice. We would do this given the likelihood that all newly created forks would contain the same content. In addition, if the reported network that contains the allegedly infringing content is larger than one hundred (100) repositories and thus would be difficult to review in its entirety, we may consider disabling the entire network if you state in your notice that, "Based on the representative number of forks I have reviewed, I believe that all or most of the forks are infringing to the same extent as the parent repository." Your sworn statement would apply to this statement.

## What are Appeals and Reinstatements?

Both Appeals and Reinstatements may arise in relation to decisions to disable or limit access to content or an account, including decisions whether or not to:

* Remove, disable access to, or restrict visibility of content
* Suspend or terminate access to an account
* Suspend or terminate access to the service, in whole or in part

An “Appeal” is where a user disputes that a violation has occurred and can provide additional information to show that a different decision should have been reached.

turns.question: 我丢失了所有双重认证和恢复方式，可以让客服凭身份证帮我恢复账号吗？

不可以。根据 GitHub 账号恢复政策：

- 出于安全原因，如果账号启用了双重认证，而你又丢失了双重认证凭据或账号恢复方式，**GitHub 支持团队不会为你恢复账号访问权限**；你必须使用官方提供的现有账号恢复方式 [1]。

建议先确认是否还能使用官方恢复方法（如已验证的设备、SSH 令牌或个人访问令牌等自动化恢复流程）；如果所有方法都无法使用，你将永久失去该账号的访问权限 [2]。

此外还可以做的是：将邮箱地址从被锁定账号中解除关联，以便用它创建新账号或用于其他已有账号 [2]。需要注意的是，GitHub 支持也不会恢复被锁定账号中的内容（公开内容你可以自行克隆或 fork）[3]。

## Can I open a support ticket to recover my account?

For security reasons, **GitHub Support will not restore access to accounts with two-factor authentication enabled if you lose your two-factor authentication credentials or lose access to your account recovery methods.** You must use existing [account recovery methods](/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa/recovering-your-account-if-you-lose-your-2fa-credentials).

GitHub does not support any other means of account recovery, including social or ID verification, by members of GitHub’s staff. This policy is in place to protect your account from unauthorized access through social engineering.

citations.title: GitHub Account Recovery Policy
citations.content:
GitHub provides [a number of account recovery methods](/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa/recovering-your-account-if-you-lose-your-2fa-credentials) including an [automated recovery process](/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa/recovering-your-account-if-you-lose-your-2fa-credentials#authenticating-with-a-verified-device-ssh-token-or-personal-access-token) if you have lost access to your GitHub.com account. **If you cannot use any of the provided recovery methods, you have permanently lost access to your account.**

You can, however, [unlink email addresses](/account-and-profile/setting-up-and-managing-your-personal-account-on-github/managing-your-personal-account/unlinking-your-email-address-from-a-locked-account) from a locked account in order to create a new account or use the email on another existing account.

citations.heading: Can I recover the contents of a user or organization account I lost access to?
citations.content:
## Can I recover the contents of a user or organization account I lost access to?

If you have lost access to a user account, you may [clone](/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/cloning-a-repository) or [fork](/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/working-with-forks/fork-a-repo) any content that is public.

If you have lost access to an organization account, you may clone or fork any content that is public and you may be able to request that remaining members of the organization clone or fork any private content.

GitHub Support will not recover the contents of a user or organization account that is locked.
